sentences.text: Gasparinisaura was a small, bipedal herbivore that lived during the Late Cretaceous.
In 2010, Gregory S. Paul estimated the animal measured 1.7 meters long and weighed 13 kilograms.
It possessed unique, low, plate-like triangular chevrons on its tail that expanded toward the back, a trait found only in Euornithopoda.
Gastroliths associated with three juvenile specimens were described in 2008, representing about 0.3% of the animal's total body weight.
This mass was considered sufficient to function as a gastric mill, unlike in sauropods where such stones are often too light.
The first fossils were discovered in 1992 near Cinco Saltos in Río Negro Province, Argentina, from the Anacleto Formation dating to about 83 million years ago.
The genus name Gasparinisaura honors the Argentine paleontologist Zulma Brandoni de Gasparini.
Three additional specimens were described in 1997, representing juvenile individuals.
Phylogenetic analysis places Gasparinisaura within the clade Elasmaria, a group of hypsilophodonts known from South America, Antarctica, and possibly Australia.
Originally, the describers considered it to be a very basal iguanodontian and the most primitive member of the clade Euiguanodontia, and it could be the most basal member of the Elasmaria group.
In 2026, Dieudonné, Paulina-Carabajal, and Cruzado-Caballero redescribed the skull anatomy and named a new clade, Dysalotosaurinae, within Dryosauridae.
The species name cincosaltensis refers to the location Cinco Saltos.
